title: Future Cybersecurity: Hardware Memory Safety, Automated Governance and Post-Quantum Cryptography
gist: Chris Swan argues security is shifting from human vigilance to automated, system-level defenses: hardware memory safety (CHERI) over mass Rust rewrites, SBOMs driven by the EU CRA, crypto-agility for post-quantum migration, and least-privilege controls for exploding agent identities. AI both accelerates exploitation and may eventually exhaust a finite vulnerability pool.

insights.claim: Chris Swan argues CHERI-style hardware capability checks, which raise exceptions on out-of-bounds memory access, are a cheaper path to memory safety than rewriting legacy C/C++ in Rust, since existing code mostly needs only a recompile.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Hardware-enforced safety favors chip and ISA vendors that adopt it over rewrite-services demand.

insights.claim: Scale of the rewrite problem: roughly 5.5 billion lines of open source C/C++ versus about 70 million lines of Rust, making a full rewrite near-impossible in useful time even with AI assistance.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Caps the realistic pace of Rust migration as a security fix; legacy code persists for decades.
insights.locator: But if you look at the size of the problem

insights.claim: Rust rewrites can introduce new logical flaws; the Rust coreutils rewrite discarded decades of hard-won experience and produced functionally equivalent replacements with new bugs.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Memory safety is not security; rewrite programs carry regression risk.
insights.locator: The rewrite of some of the coreutils

insights.claim: Latest iPhone and flagship Android SoCs (Pixel, some Galaxy) already include hardware memory-safety features cherry-picked from CHERI, activated by their OS versions.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Hardware memory safety is already arriving in premium silicon first.

insights.claim: The RISC-V Android profile is not yet finalized, so CHERI could still be included; that would bring memory safety to entry and mid-level phones and tablets and drive ubiquity.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: A standards window on RISC-V could make memory safety a commodity feature rather than a premium one.

insights.claim: Swan says CHERI missed its chance to enter Android on Arm the first time, and RISC-V offers a second attempt.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Arm ecosystem lost a differentiation window; RISC-V openness is a strategic asset.
insights.locator: CHERI kind of just missed the boat

insights.claim: Anchoring software protections to hardware, as Edera does for containers, will become more important.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Hardware-rooted container isolation is a growing security product niche.

insights.claim: Swan argues the number of vulnerabilities in software is finite, so AI-powered discovery could eventually exhaust most of them and reduce zero-day anxiety.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Contrarian long-run view: AI-driven bug hunting ends in a defender-favorable equilibrium.
insights.locator: ultimately a finite number of vulnerabilities

insights.claim: A roughly 20-year-old Microsoft Research USENIX Security paper (does software age like milk or wine) modeled latent vulnerabilities statistically, which could now be used to estimate and grind through remaining bugs in large code bases.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Gives a quantitative basis for estimating remaining vulnerability inventory.
insights.locator: does software age like milk or wine

insights.claim: Curl is cited as a real-world project where AI tools have accelerated finding many more vulnerabilities faster.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Open-source maintainers are early evidence of AI-driven vuln discovery volume.

insights.claim: LLMs are both threat and opportunity: attackers act faster at larger scale, while defenders use models such as Project Glasswing to find flaws ahead of attackers.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Security spend is shifting to AI-assisted offense and defense in parallel.

insights.claim: Developers increasingly ask their coding assistant to run security evaluations of source code (white box testing) as standard practice, instead of a late-stage pen test.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Security testing is shifting left into the AI coding workflow.

insights.claim: The last Microsoft Patch Tuesday bundle contained around a thousand patches, and AI lets attackers turn them into exploits quickly, shortening the window between disclosure or rumor and exploitation.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Patch latency becomes a direct risk driver; automated patching tooling gains value.

insights.claim: The Hugging Face incident, in which supposedly agents run amok broke into services, marks an escalation in the exploitation landscape; a CISO likened it to 10,000 drunk house robbers arriving at once.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Scale of weak agent attackers is itself a threat model.

insights.claim: Today's agent attackers are the worst they will ever be; future ones will be smarter and operate at larger scale.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Plan defenses for escalating autonomous attack capability.

insights.claim: The attack surface is the same for humans and agents, so good fundamental defense protects against human, AI-agent and hybrid attackers.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Fundamentals over novel AI-specific tooling.
insights.locator: attack surface area is the same

themes.theme: SBOMs, EU CRA and automated governance

insights.claim: The EU Cyber Resilience Act breach-reporting requirements just took effect, and the SBOM requirement takes effect in December next year for anyone selling software or software-containing products in the EU.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: A hard compliance date creates demand for SBOM and supply chain tooling.

insights.claim: SBOMs serve two purposes: evidence that an organization pays attention to security, and a basis for computing exposure to known vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Compliance artifacts double as operational exposure data.

insights.claim: Swan credits Josh Corman with starting SBOM mandates via US federal procurement, on the logic that buyers would pay less for software with vulnerable dependencies; he thinks the EU CRA will make it happen at wide scale.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Regulation-by-procurement spreads to market-wide practice via EU rules.
insights.locator: Josh Corman who started this off

insights.claim: A continuous delivery pipeline can generate SBOMs, SLSA attestations and OpenSSF Scorecards, giving evidence of ingredients, preparation and kitchen hygiene; building this in is not a massive effort.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Automated evidence generation favors teams with mature CI/CD.

insights.claim: Organizations with hand-cranked, ticket-driven processes are disadvantaged versus those with straight-through continuous delivery for patching and certificate renewal.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Delivery maturity is becoming a security and compliance advantage.

insights.claim: Swan's QCon security track theme: vulnerability comes from leaky abstractions beneath us, human vigilance cannot track it all, so attention must be systematized and automated.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Security tooling demand shifts toward continuous automated stack monitoring.

insights.claim: Swan expects post-quantum cryptography to be the necessary topic next year because Q day, when quantum computers can run Shor's algorithm to break RSA and elliptic curves, is getting closer.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Post-quantum migration is moving from futurist topic to near-term budget item.

insights.claim: NIST post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) are standardized, but the implementation landscape is immature: OpenSSL support exists only on bleeding-edge distributions that enterprises do not yet run.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Enterprise migration requires distro upgrades or backports, creating friction and services demand.

insights.claim: Swan expects post-quantum migration to resemble Y2K: first inventory where cryptography is deployed, then grind through updates to crypto-agile software.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Cryptographic inventory and discovery tooling is the first-wave need.

insights.claim: There is distrust of the new PQ algorithms because many failed during evaluation and one lattice scheme reportedly succumbed to a brute force attack using Anthropic's AI tools; Swan expects they probably will not hold up long-term.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Argues for crypto-agility rather than hard-coding the new algorithms.
insights.locator: succumbed to a sort of brute force attack

insights.claim: Because the algorithms may need replacing again within years, organizations should avoid baking PQ algorithms tightly into systems and prioritize crypto-agility.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Agility layers beat point implementations as a product strategy.

insights.claim: A doomsday scenario is reverse-engineered certificate authority private keys, letting attackers impersonate Let's Encrypt or Google; certificate transparency monitoring mitigates this, and CAs and roots of trust need to move to post-quantum.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Root-of-trust migration is a systemic dependency for PQ readiness.
insights.locator: private keys for the certificate authorities

insights.claim: Certificate lifespans are shrinking from a year toward 90 and then 45 days, which forces organizations to automate certificate management regardless of PQ plans.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Certificate lifecycle automation becomes mandatory spend.

insights.claim: Most organizations probably have around 10X more non-human identities than people, and agents are making that explode.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Machine identity management is a fast-growing security category.

insights.claim: AI agents should receive task-based, fine-grained least-privilege permissions with auditing, not the keys to the kingdom.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Agent authorization and audit layers are a needed control point.

insights.claim: Identity management formerly solved at enterprise level is becoming an individual-user problem, so AI will be needed to manage the permissions granted to agents (an Ouroboros).
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Consumer-level agent permissioning is an open product opportunity.

insights.claim: An example given of the human-in-the-loop problem: a zero day in Meta's Muse app bypassed macOS privacy protections because agents are given file system and privacy-setting access for convenience.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Agent convenience undermines OS-level privacy models.
